title: Soft failover & surge redispatch protocol (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working draft for a soft failover / surge redispatch protocol to handle partial or full degradation of a region while minimizing user impact and preserving state when possible. The goal is to provide a safe, reversible sequence of actions that SRE on-call can follow to shift traffic away from a degraded region, pre-warm caches and KV state on target capacity, and restore service with minimal rollback friction.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to region-level degradations that impact latency or error-rate but do not require an immediate hard-cut DNS switch (e.g., elevated p99 latency, distributed 5xx increase, partial GPU node pool saturation).
- Assumes hot and warm standby pools exist in one or more secondary regions and that routing supports weighted traffic steering both at the edge (CDN/edge LBs) and at the API routing layer.
- Assumes we have low-ttl DNS entries for emergency weighted failover (TTL <= 30s) and tooling for programmatic DNS updates (Route53 / Cloud DNS change-batch automation).
- This is NOT the hard failover playbook for catastrophic region outage (see regional-failover-oncall-playbook). Use those steps if control plane is inaccessible.

Detection signals (examples):
- p99 latency > 2x baseline for 5 minutes across >=3 availability zones
- 5xx rate > 2% of traffic for API tier or > 5% for edge tier for 3 minutes
- Host-level load: GPU queue length > 80% sustained for 10 minutes
- Autoscaler unable to provision capacity (repeated provisioning errors)
- Telemetry: circuit-breakers tripping on >= 20% of active routes

Decision matrix (quick guide):
- Green: transient blips (<3m), monitor.
- Amber: sustained degradation (>=5m) but control plane and routing healthy -> proceed with soft failover.
- Red: control plane or cross-region network fabric compromised -> escalate to hard failover.

Prerequisites (verify before executing):
- Incident channel created: #sre-ops-incidents with incident ID in topic.
- Pager/contact list available (on-call, infra owners, routing owner, product).
- Warm standby health checks pass (API health, KV connectivity, model processes) in target region.
- Pre-warm scripts available and access to run them (privileged account + ssh/exec rights).
- Route change automation tool (routing-cli) accessible from on-call workstation.

High-level plan (order of preferred actions):
1) Shift a controlled fraction of traffic (10-30%) away from degraded region to warm standby using internal routing weights.
2) Monitor error/latency signals closely for 10 minutes. If target region shows errors increase, stop and rollback weights.
3) If steady, incrementally increase traffic to 50% while running KV pre-seed and cache-warming passes in target region.
4) Once target region shows stable latency and error rates below thresholds, proceed to DNS weight adjustments (edge/Route53) to reduce dependency on degraded region.
5) Continue incremental shifts until degraded region <10% traffic then apply throttles and/or graceful drain to 0% if necessary.

Detailed steps (operator commands and checks):
A. Initial controlled internal shift (preferred):
- Run: routing-cli set-weight --route api-redwood --from-region us-west-2 --to-region eu-west-1 --weight 20
- Verify: routing-cli status --route api-redwood | grep weights
- Check: p50/p95/p99 dashboards for both source and target regions (allow 10m warm window).
- Monitor: redis/memcache miss rates, KV cache hit ratio, and model latency histograms.

B. Pre-warm KV cache and model caches on target region:
- Run prewarm job: ./scripts/prewarm-prefixes.sh --prefix-list top-100-app-prefixes --target eu-west-1
  - This issues non-user traffic to populate prefix/KV caches. Rate-limit to avoid spike.
- Start small: 50 concurrent prewarm workers, observe KV write throughput and network egress.
- Typical time: 3-7 minutes for top-100 prefixes; larger workloads may need longer.

C. DNS weighted adjustment (if edge routing weight insufficient):
- Prepare Route53 change-batch JSON with small weight shift (10-25%). TTL should be 30s or lower for emergency records.
- Example (operator): aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z12345 --change-batch file://shift-weights.json
- Verify: dig +short @8.8.8.8 api.redwood.ai -> check returned IPs/weights through edge provider APIs.

D. Sticky sessions and affinity considerations:
- If clients use long-lived sessions, ensure target region supports session affinity or apply sticky cookie forwarding. Expect uneven immediate errors for long-lived open sessions.
- Consider injecting a 302 redirect for session rehydration to force new connections when appropriate.

E. KV cache state and consistency:
- For prefix-based KV caches, prefer read-through + background pre-seed. Avoid synchronous shard replication during surge unless tested.
- If KV consistency issues detected, reduce traffic shift and run a targeted reconciliation job for hot keys.

Rollback policy and cooldowns:
- After any weight change, wait at least 10 minutes of stable metrics before additional shifts.
- If error rate rises > 50% relative to baseline in target region after shift, revert to previous snapshot and call a second opinion from routing owner.
- Cooldown window after rollback: 30 minutes before retrying changes. Document both action and timestamp in incident channel.

Communication templates (paste into Slack):
- Short alert to incident channel: "INCIDENT [ID] – us-west-2 region p99 elevated. Initiating 20% soft shift to eu-west-1 at 14:12 UTC. Prewarm started. Monitoring p99/p95. Owner: @ava. If metrics degrade, roll back."
- Update to product/CS: "We're routing a portion of traffic to standby region to mitigate elevated latency in us-west-2. Customer impact mitigated; will update in 15m."

Common pitfalls and brief mitigation notes:
- Pitfall: Forgetting to prewarm caches -> Results in spike in cold starts and high latency on target region. Mitigation: run prewarm script before increasing weights past 30%.
- Pitfall: Using DNS alone when control plane is flaky -> DNS changes may not propagate fast enough or may be rate-limited. Mitigation: prefer internal routing weights first.
- Pitfall: Overloading warm standby compute because autoscalers have different scale profiles. Mitigation: review autoscaler configs and perform staged capacity increases.

Post-incident checklist (what to collect & create):
- Time-annotated timeline of each weight change and prewarm job start/stop times.
- Dashboard snapshots (p50/p95/p99, error rates, KV hit ratios) for both regions around each change.
- Collect routing-cli and DNS change logs, and any edge provider logs for the time window.
- Open follow-up Jira: SRE-xxxx for root cause analysis and runbook improvements. Attach runbook gaps.

Dry-run notes (recent test):
- Dry-run date: 2025-02-28 09:00 UTC (small internal test with low-traffic canary).
- Actions: 15% shift from us-west-2 -> eu-west-1, prewarm run for top-50 prefixes.
- Observations:
  - Prewarm completed in 4m 20s; KV write TPS peaked at expected margin (60 TPS), no errors.
  - Target region p99 rose 10% briefly during prewarm but returned to baseline within 6m.
  - Autoscaler for model workers needed a config tweak (min_replicas was 2; bump to 4 required for sustained 50% shift). Created Jira: SRE-1203.
- Learnings applied: add autoscaler sanity check to prerequisites and reduce prewarm concurrency default from 100 -> 50.

Runbook maintenance guidance (how to keep this doc useful):
- Mark as draft until three successful dry-runs recorded and validated by routing owner.
- After any real incident use, update timeline, add exact CLI command outputs, and capture any edge-provider fallout (e.g., rate limits).
- Schedule quarterly tabletop exercises for SRE and routing team to rehearse this flow.

Quick on-call cheatsheet (to paste into incident post):
- Step 0: Create incident channel, confirm contacts.
- Step 1: Confirm degraded metrics and escalate to amber.
- Step 2: Ensure warm standby health checks green.
- Step 3: Apply 10-20% internal weight shift (routing-cli).
- Step 4: Prewarm KV caches; watch KV hit ratio and model cold-starts.
- Step 5: Incremental shifts with 10m observation windows.
- Step 6: If stable, adjust DNS weights; otherwise rollback and open follow-ups.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Add automated prewarm orchestration into routing-cli so prewarm is invoked automatically on weight > 30%.
- Verify edge provider limits on weighted DNS changes; document per-provider throttles.
- Define minimum warm-standby capacity profiles for each customer tier (free/prod/enterprise).

Owner notes:
- This is intentionally lightweight and reversible. The emphasis is on small increments, prewarming, and clear rollback signals. Please comment in the incident channel or assign edits in the linked PR.

Last test/runbook edit log:
- 2025-02-11: Initial draft by Ava Martinez.
- 2025-02-28: Dry-run recorded; autoscaler note added (Owen Reyes).
- 2025-03-04: Added DNS and rollback clarifications (Marcus Chen).
